{{Short description|Class of prime numbers}}
An '''emirp''' (pronounced {{IPAc-en|'|i:|m|@r|p}} or {{IPAc-en|'|E|m|@r|p}}, an [[anadrome]] of ''prime'') is a [[prime number]] that results in a different prime when its [[decimal]] digits ([[Numerical digit|digits]] in base 10) are reversed.<ref name="mathworld">{{MathWorld|title=Emirp|urlname=Emirp}}</ref> This definition excludes the related [[palindromic prime]]s. The term '''''reversible prime''''' is used to mean the same as emirp, but may also, ambiguously, include the palindromic primes.

The first few emirps are

:13, 17, 31, 37, 71, 73, 79, 97, 107, 113, 149, 157, 167, 179, 199, ... {{OEIS|id=A006567}}.

The first few reversible primes are

:2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 31, 37, 71, 73, 79, 97, 101, 107, ... {{OEIS|id=A007500}}.

The difference in all pairs of emirps is always a multiple of 18. This follows from all primes bigger than 2 being odd (making their differences even, i.e. multiples of 2) and from differences between pairs of natural numbers with reversed digits being multiples of 9 (which itself is a consequence of <math>10^n-1</math> being a multiple of 9 for every non-negative integer <math>n</math>).

All non-palindromic [[permutable prime]]s are emirps.

It is not known whether there are infinitely many emirps. The largest ''known'' emirp as of April 19, 2026 is {{nowrap|10<sup>111956</sup> - 7 × 10<sup>53855</sup> - 1}} by Ryan Propper and Serge Batalov.<ref name="rivera">{{cite web |first1=Carlos |last1=Rivera |title=Puzzle 20. - Reversible Primes |website=Prime Puzzles |url=https://www.primepuzzles.net/puzzles/puzz_020.htm |access-date=5 August 2026}}</ref> The integer's reverse is {{nowrap|10<sup>111956</sup> - 7 × 10<sup>58100</sup> - 1}}.

== History ==
The term "emirp" was coined by American mathematician [[Jeremiah Farrell]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A006567}}</ref>

The number of ''n''-digit reversible primes is equal to the number of ''n''-digit emirps plus the number of ''n''-digit palindromic primes.

== Other bases ==

Emirps also exist for bases other than 10. For example, 10111<sub>2</sub> = 23 is an emirp in the [[binary numeral system]] because 23 is a prime and its reverse 11101<sub>2</sub> = 29 is also a prime.

The first few binary emirps are

:11, 13, 23, 29, 37, 41, 43, 47, 53, 61, 67, 71, 83, 97, 101, ... {{OEIS|id=A080790}}.

Dartyge et al. (2023) have shown that, in [[big-O notation]], the number of ''n''-digit reversible primes in binary is <math>O\left(\frac{2^n}{n^2}\right)</math>.

They also conjecture that the number of ''n''-digit reversible primes in binary is <math>(3+o(1))\frac{2^{n-1}}{(\log2^n)^2}</math> as ''n'' goes large.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Dartyge |first1=Cécile |last2=Martin |first2=Bruno |last3=Rivat |first3=Joël |last4=Shparlinski |first4=Igor |last5=Swaenepoel |first5=Cathy |title=Reversible primes |year=2023 |arxiv=2309.11380 |class=math.NT }}</ref>

== Emirpimes ==

The term '''emirpimes''' (singular) is used also in places to treat [[semiprime]]s in a similar way. That is, an emirpimes is a semiprime that is also a (distinct) semiprime upon reversing its digits.<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Emirpimes|urlname=Emirpimes}}</ref>

The first few emirpimeses are

:15, 26, 39, 49, 51, 58, 62, 85, 93, 94, 115, 122, 123, ... {{OEIS|id=A097393}}.
